analysis.one_liner: Strips baseball's antitrust exemption for pooling its television broadcast rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in the House Judiciary Committee and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1961, professional sports leagues — including baseball — have been exempt from antitrust laws when they bundle and sell all their teams' TV rights as one package. This bill would have ended that protection for baseball, letting antitrust laws apply to those deals like they apply to other businesses. It was introduced the day after the 1994 baseball strike's standoff and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Fans and viewers could gain if competition among broadcasters increases — more games offered on more channels, and potentially better terms for consumers. Competing networks and upstart sports broadcasters could also gain access to baseball content that is currently packaged exclusively by the league. Owners would face the risk of antitrust suits over jointly negotiated TV contracts.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961 by striking "baseball" from the exemption and adding a section making antitrust laws apply to joint baseball agreements of the kind covered by the act [S3].
The bill would take effect on enactment, but pre-existing joint TV agreements would keep working for one year before the new rules apply [S3].
The CRS summary describes the bill as excluding professional baseball from the antitrust exemption applicable to the telecasting of professional sports contests [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Major League Baseball and its 30 club owners, who would lose the ability to negotiate all teams' national TV rights as a single package free from antitrust challenge. That pooled bargaining typically maximizes what networks pay for exclusive rights, and owners would bear both litigation risk and potentially lower rights revenue.

drawbacks.text: The Sports Broadcasting Act exemption exists because pooled, exclusive league-wide TV packages were thought to keep games on free over-the-air television and protect attendance from TV-driven competition; removing the exemption could fragment broadcasts and push games toward pay television or streaming.

The bill is narrow: it touches only the television-telecasting exemption and leaves baseball's separate, century-old antitrust exemption for the reserve system and franchise relocation untouched, so its practical effect on fans and players is limited [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would remove a real special privilege — baseball is the only major sport carved into the 1961 TV antitrust exemption by name — and exposing pooled TV deals to competition could benefit viewers. But the stakes are modest for most households: the everyday effect would be felt through what games appear on which channels and how much networks pay for rights, not in wages, prices, or health coverage. The bill's narrowness also means it would not address the larger antitrust issues in baseball, like the reserve clause.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Bilirakis introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the first day of the 104th Congress [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary that same day [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded; the bill attracted no cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major League Baseball owners, who kept their antitrust protection for pooled television rights. Viewers and competing broadcasters lost the chance to see those deals tested by antitrust law.

for.name: Rep. Michael Bilirakis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip baseball's TV antitrust exemption

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — during the two-year Congress

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors; no vote was ever taken, so no party split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Major League Baseball (team owners and the league office)
industries.note: The bill would end baseball's antitrust protection for bundling all teams' national TV rights into exclusive packages, exposing those contracts to antitrust suits. The exemption lets the league restrict how many and where games are broadcast, which limits what fans can watch.

Networks that currently bid on exclusive league-wide packages could face more competition for baseball rights, while incumbent rights-holders could lose the exclusivity that makes their contracts valuable. Viewers could see games spread across more outlets.
